content.title: About
content.content: Baby Toddler Juice, Apple is a 100 % natural apple juice specially formulated for children from 1 year old. It contains no added sugar, preservatives or artificial flavors and is enriched with vitamin C and iron to support growth and development.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Apple juice is one of the most popular toddler drinks thanks to its mild taste and high nutritional value.
The juice is made from selected apple varieties grown without pesticides.
Each 100 ml provides about 45 mg of vitamin C – more than 50 % of the daily requirement for children.
The juice is pasteurized at low temperature to preserve maximum vitamins and aroma compounds.
Packaging is made from safe, reusable plastic.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system, aids iron absorption and protects cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Source of natural sugars
items.content: Contains fructose and glucose that provide quick energy without added sugar.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Iron is essential for hemoglobin formation and helps prevent anemia in children.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: A small amount of dietary fiber helps regulate bowel movements.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: The juice contributes to daily fluid intake, especially in warm weather.

items.title: Apple allergy
items.content: A small number of children may experience an allergic reaction to apple juice.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: High acidity can irritate a sensitive stomach in some toddlers; diluting the juice with water is recommended.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Although no added sugar is present, natural sugars are still there; intake should be monitored.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the juice chilled in small portions (50–100 ml) right after meals or between meals. For younger children, dilute the juice with water in a 1:1 ratio.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in the refrigerator at 2–4 °C. Once opened, consume within 3–5 days. Do not freeze.

chicken-or-turkey-and-noodles-with-mushr.title: Chicken or turkey with noodles in mushroom sauce

content.title: About
content.content: The dish consists of selected chicken or turkey fillet, boiled noodles and a delicate mushroom sauce made from cream and button mushrooms. Cooking keeps the meat juicy while the sauce adds an aromatic, slightly creamy mushroom flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken and turkey are lean protein sources often used in diet nutrition.
Traditional mushroom sauce is made with button mushrooms, but white or oyster mushrooms can be added for a richer taste.
Noodles are usually cooked al dente to retain texture and not become soggy in the sauce.
The dish is popular in both Asian and European cuisines as a quick lunch or dinner.
Creamy mushroom sauce is often seasoned with garlic, thyme or rosemary.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Chicken and turkey provide high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low in saturated fat (especially turkey)
items.content: Poultry fillets contain little saturated fat, making the dish suitable for heart‑healthy diets.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Poultry is abundant in niacin, vitamin B6 and B12, supporting metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Mushrooms provide vitamin D and selenium
items.content: Button mushrooms contain vitamin D, important for bone health, and selenium, an antioxidant.

items.title: Carbohydrates from noodles give energy
items.content: Noodles supply a quick source of energy, especially useful after physical activity.

items.title: Mushroom allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to mushrooms.

items.title: Sodium content in the sauce
items.content: Prepared creamy sauces can be salty; monitor added salt.

items.title: Processed ingredients
items.content: If using a ready‑made sauce, check for preservatives and artificial flavors.

items.title: Thorough cooking required
items.content: Poultry must be fully cooked to avoid the risk of salmonella.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot, garnished with fresh herbs such as parsley or dill. A sprinkle of grated Parmesan or a dash of hot sauce can be added to taste. It pairs well with a light fresh‑vegetable salad.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool leftovers within 2 hours of cooking and store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Reheat thoroughly until steaming hot to ensure the meat is fully warmed.

egg-omelet-or-scrambled-egg-with-cheese-.title: Egg omelet with cheese and tomatoes, no added fat

content.title: About
content.content: This dish consists of beaten eggs cooked without added oil or butter, combined with low‑fat cream cheese and fresh tomatoes. It can be prepared on a dry skillet or in a microwave, keeping the calorie count low while preserving flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Eggs are a complete protein source, containing all essential amino acids.
Low‑fat cream cheese adds a creamy texture and calcium without many extra calories.
Tomatoes are rich in lycopene, which becomes more bioavailable after heating.
Cooking without added fat reduces saturated fat and calories to about 150 kcal per serving.
The dish is quick to make—usually 5–7 minutes on the stovetop.

items.title: High protein content
items.content: One serving provides roughly 6–7 g of high‑quality protein, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Rich in vitamin D and B12
items.content: Eggs supply vitamin D and vitamin B12, important for bone health and nervous system function.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: Cream cheese contributes calcium, beneficial for bones and teeth.

items.title: Lycopene from tomatoes
items.content: Heat‑processed tomatoes increase lycopene availability, an antioxidant supportive of heart health.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: The absence of added oil makes the dish suitable for low‑fat dietary plans.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Individuals with egg allergy should avoid this dish.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Eggs contain cholesterol; people with high cholesterol should monitor portion size.

items.title: Sodium in cheese
items.content: Some cream cheeses are salty; choose low‑sodium versions if you have hypertension.

items.title: Risk of foodborne illness
items.content: Eggs should be fully cooked to eliminate the risk of salmonella.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the omelet hot, optionally garnished with fresh herbs and a pinch of black pepper. It can be eaten on its own, rolled in a flatbread, or paired with whole‑grain toast.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Best enjoyed immediately. If needed, store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours; reheat before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: A peanut butter and jelly sandwich is made with two slices of white bread, a thin layer of reduced‑fat peanut butter, and sweet fruit jelly. It is a popular quick snack often found in schools and cafés.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first peanut butter and jelly sandwich recipes appeared in the United States in the early 1900s.
Reduced‑fat peanut butter typically contains about 30 % fat instead of 50 % in regular versions.
White bread is chosen for its soft texture that holds the filling well.
The sweet jelly and slightly salty butter create a flavor balance that stimulates saliva production.
The sandwich can be easily customized with banana, honey, or nuts.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: Peanut butter provides about 8 g of protein per 100 g, helping maintain muscle mass.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: The reduced‑fat version contains less saturated fat, which is better for heart health.

items.title: Source of vitamin E
items.content: Vitamin E in peanut butter acts as an antioxidant, protecting cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: White bread and jelly add a modest amount of fiber, supporting digestion.

items.title: Quick source of energy
items.content: Carbohydrates from the bread and sugar in the jelly rapidly replenish glycogen stores.

items.title: Peanut allergy
items.content: Peanut butter can trigger severe allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Jelly often contains added sugar, which may be problematic for diabetes or weight management.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: White bread raises blood glucose quickly, so people with blood‑sugar concerns should opt for whole‑grain bread.

items.title: Added salt
items.content: Some reduced‑fat peanut butter brands add salt; those monitoring sodium intake should check the label.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Spread a thin layer of peanut butter on one slice of bread, evenly distribute the jelly, and top with the second slice. Optionally cut the sandwich into halves or quarters for easier handling.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the assembled sandwich in an airtight container at room temperature for no more than 4 hours. Store opened peanut butter and jelly in the refrigerator, and keep bread in a dry place.

content.title: About
content.content: Egg quesadilla is a Mexican dish consisting of a thin corn or wheat tortilla filled with scrambled egg and often complemented by cheese, vegetables, and spices. It cooks quickly, is nutritious, and works well for breakfast or a light dinner.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The word “quesadilla” comes from the Spanish “queso,” meaning cheese, although the original version may omit cheese.
Adding egg makes the dish more filling and provides a high‑quality protein source, popular among athletes.
Tortillas used can be corn or wheat, influencing flavor and texture.
In Mexico, quesadillas are commonly served with salsa, guacamole, and sour cream.
Fast preparation time (about 5‑7 minutes) makes it a favorite for busy people.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Eggs provide high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs contain B2, B6, and B12 vitamins that support energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Healthy fats
items.content: When cheese is added, the dish includes monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats beneficial for heart health.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Eggs and tortillas supply iron, zinc, and phosphorus, important for bones and immunity.

items.title: Low in carbs
items.content: Egg quesadilla fits moderate low‑carb diets, especially when using whole‑grain tortillas.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to eggs, ranging from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Eggs contain cholesterol; people with high cholesterol should monitor their intake.

items.title: Salt and fat in add‑ons
items.content: Cheese and sauces can increase sodium and saturated fat levels, which should be considered in a balanced diet.

items.title: Tortilla quality
items.content: Refined‑flour tortillas have a higher glycemic index; whole‑grain options are preferable.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat a skillet and lightly oil it. Place a tortilla, spread beaten egg over it, add shredded cheese and any vegetables (tomatoes, spinach, bell pepper). Fold the tortilla in half and cook until golden and the cheese melts, about 2‑3 minutes per side.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Best enjoyed fresh. Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. Reheat in a skillet or oven to retain a crisp crust.

content.title: About
content.content: A beef and cheese taco is a classic Mexican dish consisting of a corn tortilla filled with seasoned ground beef, melted cheese, and often topped with onions, cilantro, and salsa. The corn tortilla gives a distinct flavor and a slightly crunchy texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Corn tortillas have been used in Mexico for over 3,000 years.
The word “taco” entered English usage in the early 20th century.
Traditional taco beef is marinated in lime juice and spices such as cumin and chili powder.
In the United States more than 4 billion tacos are consumed each year.
While cheddar is common in the U.S., Mexican tacos often use queso fresco or cotija.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Beef provides a complete source of protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Rich in iron
items.content: Beef supplies easily absorbed heme iron, supporting healthy hemoglobin levels.

items.title: Corn tortilla offers fiber
items.content: Corn flour contains dietary fiber that aids digestion.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: Cheese adds calcium, important for bone and teeth health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Beef and cheese are good sources of B12, B6, and niacin, which support the nervous system.

items.title: High saturated fat
items.content: Large amounts of cheese and fatty beef can raise cholesterol if eaten frequently.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Seasonings and cheese often contain a lot of salt, which may be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Cheese can trigger allergic reactions in people with lactose intolerance or dairy allergy.

items.title: Pathogen contamination
items.content: Undercooked beef may harbor Salmonella or E. coli.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve tacos hot, folding the tortilla in half. Top with fresh cilantro, lime wedges, salsa, guacamole, or sour cream. For a lighter version, use lean beef and low‑fat cheese.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store prepared tacos in the refrigerator in an airtight container for up to 2 days. Keep dry tortillas in a sealed bag at room temperature. Beef can be frozen for up to 3 months, and cheese for up to 2 months.
